# [Food Labeling: Principles to support the uptake of healthy and sustainable diets](https://www.wbcsd.org/Programs/Food-and-Nature/Food-Land-Use/FReSH/Resources/Food-Labeling-Principles-to-support-the-uptake-of-healthy-and-sustainable-diets) *(report - 2021)*

  - The World Business Council for Sustainable Development (WBCSD) [released a report in November 2021](https://www.wbcsd.org/contentwbc/download/13275/194329/1) that **includes a high-level assessment of existing nutrition and environmental impact labels**, **and factors that may affect their efficacy and uptake**
  - The report updates and builds upon information from the WBCSD’s [2020 chapter on Healthy and Sustainable Diets](https://www.wbcsd.org/Programs/Food-and-Nature/Food-Land-Use/FReSH/Resources/Food-Agriculture-Roadmap-Chapter-on-Healthy-and-Sustainable-Diets) (part of its [Food and Agriculture Roadmap](https://www.wbcsd.org/Programs/Food-and-Nature/Food-Land-Use/Food-Agriculture-Roadmap)), in light of the fact that the use of food labeling systems has expanded significantly since its publication
  - **It provides detailed information regarding \*\*attributes of eight types of environmental scoring labels and six types of nutrition scoring labels\*\***
  - The report adapts the ten principles in the [United Nations Guidelines for Providing Product Sustainability Information](https://wedocs.unep.org/bitstream/handle/20.500.11822/22180/guidelines_product_sust_info.pdf?sequence=1&isAllowed=y) (2017) for nutrition and environmental impact scoring labels for food
  - It also includes **nine recommendations on best practices for driving behavior change** through food impact scoring, including recommendations to label non-packaged products, to aggregate details into straightforward and concise information, and to use scientific evidence that has strong international consensus

  

### [Fast Company — Brands are starting to add carbon labels to their packaging](https://www.fastcompany.com/90609538/brands-are-starting-to-add-carbon-labels-to-their-packaging) *(magazine article - 2021)*

  - **Carbon labeling is a growing trend**, increasingly on track to become (more) mainstream as companies begin to internally measure the climate impact of their products, and then communicate it externally—placing the burden of education on the brand and not on the consumer 
  - Article offers a number of examples and detailed anecdotes to support the claims, namely Cocokind, Oatly, Unilever, Just Salad—demonstrating that **the growing trend extends across categories**
  - However, it’s **challenging to accurately calculate carbon footprint data**, as that of any singular product changes constantly due to a number of fluctuating variables (e.g. time of year, source, shelf life, etc.)—meaning that **carbon labeling is a calculation, not a scientific measurement**. 
  - An additional challenge is that, until carbon labeling is standardized and ubiquitous, data can be difficult to compare, and thus **hard for consumers to interpret and use**. As carbon labeling becomes more widespread, and as innovation leads to more tools that increase accessibility and digestibility, **usefulness will be increased**

  

### [HelloFresh launches climate labeling to help customers make more sustainable recipe choices](https://www.foodnavigator.com/Article/2021/11/09/HelloFresh-launches-climate-labelling-to-help-customers-make-more-sustainable-recipe-choices?mc_cid=5f5d8618e8&mc_eid=5c5014c674) *(NSP - 2021)*

### [Consumers underestimate the emissions associated with food but are aided by labels](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41558-018-0354-z.epdf?author_access_token=ZXWI0btyZIWQwj7rLOmtntRgN0jAjWel9jnR3ZoTv0NsSCbRFysgh2dTg6tP9Ljh3ZPfMqfetXSOGIC-loyi9eSLPa_3h1Oh2J4xrzN9fuDn2ABJwxsSNwutYvhREct9TXGhEj9cBajpa94vlPahBw%3D%3D) *(academic paper - 2019)*

*By researchers at UTS Business School, University of Technology Sydney, published in* Nature Climate Change, Vol. 9 

  - **Diet change is an important behavioral strategy for reducing environmental impacts** associated with high levels of energy use and GHG emissions released by food production
  - **A substantial obstacle to food behavior change is consumers’ poor understanding of the food system and lack of awareness around its connection with GHG emissions**—energy consumption and GHG emission estimates are significantly underestimated for foods
  - However, **when provided with information regarding these emissions, presented in terms of a familiar reference unit (light-bulb minutes), consumers make this connection and demonstrably shift their actual purchase choices towards lower-emission options**.
      
      - Note that labels are effective in changing consumers’ purchase decisions only when they provide information that is easy to understand/ explicit
  - This illustrates that current barriers to food behavior change can be **mediated through simple interventions such as well-designed carbon label**s
      
      - An effective carbon label should be simple to understand and include reference values that permit comparisons and put information in context
  - Additional commentary is offered here in a [post](https://centers.fuqua.duke.edu/edge/2018/12/19/new-faculty-research-the-carbon-footprint-of-the-food-we-eat/) for the Duke Fuqua School of Business.

  

### [Interested, indifferent or active information avoiders of carbon labels: Cognitive dissonance and ascription of responsibility as motivating factors](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1PWdZPVQ0Zs6hq_f7cwBu1QX3QxiE3ZFA/view?usp=sharing) *(academic paper - 2021)*

*Article on Food policy in Elsevier*

  

*Overview:* In this article, **we investigate whether consumers actively avoid information about the climate impact of food products, and we explore motivations for such active avoidance.** 

  

  - We test whether conflicting cognitions and responsibility feelings in the domain of climate change affects food choices when exposed to CO2e information. 
  - We identify consumers who wish to avoid climate impact information, but when such information is imposed upon them, change their purchase behavior towards lower emissions products. 
  - Moreover, we explore how conflicting cognitions and responsibility feelings affect choice behavior and choice uncertainty when climate impact information is provided, and if this motivates active information avoidance.
  - In the first stage of a stated preference survey, respondents indicated whether they wished to access carbon emissions information (info-takers) or not (info-decliners) when selecting a protein source. In the second stage, all respondents were provided with carbon emissions information. **The info-takers reduced emissions from their food choices by 32%, while the info-decliners also reduced their emissions (by 12%)**. This indicates active information avoidance among at least some info-decliners.

  

*Methods:* An online survey was distributed by a research panel firm in Sweden, resulting in 803 responses. The survey included initial screening questions on sociodemographic characteristics, which were used to ensure a representative sample of the population with respect to gender, age and region. Next, there were questions regarding food-related habits and general food attitudes, followed by the choice tasks. A final section included questions regarding attitudes and beliefs, for measuring CD and R\&N, detailed further below.

  

*Results:* The study reveals that **some individuals avoid carbon information where possible, yet alter their behavior if the information is imposed upon them**. These findings point to the potential of **increasing impact from information by simultaneously increasing personal responsibility feelings and activating social norms**.

  

  - The implication from our findings is that while interested individuals can be expected to more actively seek out climate impact information (e.g., turn the package, read a complex label), avoiders will only be affected by the label if it is imposed upon them. Hence, **while CO2e can be reduced by providing consumers with labels on their products, such initiatives will likely need to be mandatory**, because high-emissions producers are unlikely to voluntarily provide such information on a product level. 
  - **Our findings imply that the impact of climate information hinges on consumers' underlying motivations**.The study demonstrates that, when positive beliefs and preferences towards carbon-heavy consumption are combined with climate concerns, carbon emissions information results in greater uncertainty in choice behavior. Similarly, responsibility feelings and norms that move a person to transition to climate-friendly consumption result in increased choice uncertainty when exposed to climate impact information. **For greater behavioral changes from information measures such as labels, it is promising to focus on activating moral obligations and responsibility feelings.** 
  - An interesting way forward would be to explore interventions that, in combination with in- formation provision, evoke feelings of responsibility, possibly through evoking pride or guilt (Vermeir et al., 2020). In addition, increased cognitive dissonance has the potential to increase behavioral change, possibly by emphasizing the discrepancy between the problem (large climate impact from certain food products) and one’s personal actions.

  

### [Panera Bread becomes first national chain to label entrees as climate friendly](https://www.cnbc.com/2020/10/14/panera-bread-to-label-entrees-as-climate-friendly.html) *(NSP - 2020)*

  

  - A decade ago, Panera was the first national chain to implement calorie labeling

  - [Methodology:](https://www.panerabread.com/en-us/articles/climate-friendly-meals.html) **Meals with the badge have a lower carbon footprint than the standard American diet.** If emissions are below a maximum per-meal GHG threshold, as developed by WRI--and based on a daily maximum recommended carbon footprint for a person’s diet, with 20% max coming from breakfast, 30% max from lunch, and 30% max from dinner--and if it meets a nutritional safeguard (Nutri-Score), it earns the Cool Food Meal badge.
      
      - WRI uses the ingredients list to calculate the dish’s carbon footprint based on the agricultural supply chain and land use to produce the meal.

# [Identifying Cool Food Meals](https://files.wri.org/s3fs-public/identifying-cool-food-meals.pdf) *(report - 2020)*

*Technical note, WRI*

  

**Cool Food is a global initiative that aims to help food providers sell dishes with smaller climate footprints.** This technical note outlines the methods used by World Resources Institute (WRI) to identify a set of Cool Food Meals on a food provider’s menu. 

  

  - Drawing on the calculation methods established under the Cool Food Pledge, Cool Food Meals **must fall under a maximum threshold of per-meal greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions** based on recipe data submitted to WRI (at least 38 percent below the regional

average diet). 

  - In addition, Cool Food Meals are **subject to a nutrition safeguard to ensure they meet a minimum threshold of nutritional quality**. 
  - Designation of Cool Food Meals is open to food providers that are Cool Food Pledge members, Cool Food “Heroes” who serve an especially low-GHG-emitting menu, or food providers for whom at least 20 percent of annual sales are dishes that qualify as Cool Food Meals. Both designations aim to help consumers choose dishes that contribute to an overall diet in greater alignment with 2030 targets for food-related GHG emissions reduction.
  - These **initiatives and accompanying marketing campaigns aim to steer consumers toward the low-emitting options on menus**, help shift the market toward climate-friendly food providers, and inspire others across the food service industry to accelerate the transition toward a sustainable food future. 

  

***Recommendation:*** **Publicly recognizing climate-friendly food providers, and steering consumers toward low-emitting menu options, can help accelerate the transition toward a sustainable food future.**

### [A Meta-analysis of Food Labeling Effects on Consumer Diet Behaviors and Industry Practices](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6340779/pdf/nihms-1512194.pdf) *(academic paper - 2019)*

  

*Research article published In* American Journal of Preventive Medicine*; Performed as part of the* [*Food Price Project*](https://www.food-price.org/)

  

  - *Goal/objective:* To better understand the influence of food and beverage labeling on consumer behaviors, industry responses, and diet-related health outcomes, this research project sought to pool quantitative findings across all research done to-date.
      
      - (\*Though because of heterogeneity across the outcomes in the studies analyzed, quantitative meta-analysis of health outcomes in the end could not be performed)
  - *Methodology:* Researchers systematically reviewed all relevant studies (i.e. those that explored these questions) published between 1990-2014
  - *Results:* Analysis of the 60 intervention studies that met inclusion criteria (including 111 intervention arms and more than 2 million observations across 11 countries) showed that **food labeling reduces consumer dietary intake of selected nutrients, and influences industry practices to reduce product contents of sodium and artificial trans fat**.
      
      - *Consumer behavior*: food labeling decreased consumer intakes of energy by 6.6%, total fat by 10.6%. and other unhealthy dietary options by 13.0% Food labeling increased vegetable consumption by 13.5%. A borderline, non-statistically significant reduction was seen for sodium. Labeling did not significantly alter intakes of other dietary targets.
      - *Industry responses*: food labeling decreased product contents of sodium by 8.9% and artificial trans fat by 64.3%. Significant effects were not identified on other product contents.
      - In studies evaluating traffic light systems that included three tiers, labeling increased the selections of healthier green and mid-level, and reduced selection of less healthy red options. Evaluated in two tiers, food labeling significantly altered the percentage of healthier options selected, but not unhealthy options.
  - *Definition*: Food labeling =  package labeling and menu or other point-of-purchase labeling that offered standardized provision of nutrition content or healthfulness info

### [The Effects of Environmental Sustainability Labels on Selection, Purchase, and Consumption of Food and Drink Products: A Systematic Review](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/0013916521995473) *(academic paper - 2021)*

*Review by University of Oxford researchers, published in* Environment and Behavior

  

  - *Goal/Objective:* The researchers systematically reviewed the effect of ecolabels on the selection, purchase, and/or consumption of environmentally sustainable food and drink, both in real and hypothetical contexts. They also assessed whether any effect of ecolabels is moderated by presentation format, type of information, and/or the presence of a certification label, and whether effects vary by socio-demographic characteristics.
  - *Methodology:* Researchers systematically reviewed all relevant studies (i.e., those designed to measure effects of ecolabels on selection, purchase, and/or consumption of food or drink, using an experimental intervention) from six databases (1973-present)
  - *Results:* Analysis of the 56 studies that met inclusion criteria showed a consistent association between **ecolabeling**, in a variety of messaging formats, **with the selection and purchase of more sustainable food products** (60 out of 76 total interventions)
      
      - *Purchasing Behavior:* **Of 10 studies that tested effects on actual purchases, nine studies significantly favored the ecolabeling intervention.** Of 30 studies testing hypothetical purchases, 24 studies favored the ecolabeling intervention.
      - *\*Comparative Effectiveness:\* 11 studies directly compared two or more eligible interventions. Evidence from these studies suggests that \*\*pesticide-free, organic, waste use, and carbon footprint ecolabels are equally effective at changing consumer behavior.\*\* Additionally, \*\*providing information about the GHG emissions of a product\*\*, regardless of the level of GHG emissions presented, \*\*was found to be effective at changing behavior.\*\* Furthermore, \*\*making an ecolabel more accessible by providing a “total score” and color-coding increased its effectiveness.\*\**
      - *Ecolabel Formats*: While all ecolabel formats were found to be effective in the majority of studies, **those in logo-only or text-only format appeared more effective for environmental sustainability messages and claims** than those formats that combined logo and text information. Conversely, **the combined logo and text format appeared more effective for presenting GHG emissions information and claims. All formats were largely effective for organic claims.**
      - *\*Socio-Demographic Characteristics:\* In 10 of 15 studies that examined gender as a mediator of effectiveness, \*\*females were found to be influenced more positively than males by ecolabels.\*\* In 7 of 12 studies that examined participant income, participants with higher incomes had positive effects of greater magnitude from ecolabels. Results were mixed regarding age and education level.*

### [Improving Public Engagement With Climate Change: Five ‘Best Practice’ Insights From Psychological Science.](https://drive.google.com/file/d/16EyzOtNUlvnnYnymtGWb6mUrk7-ZbeQR/view?usp=sharing) *(academic paper - 2015)*

*Perspectives on Psychological Science 10, no. 6* 

  

In this article, researchers advance **five simple “best practice” insights from psychological science that can help governments improve public policymaking about climate change.** 

*Overview*

1.  **\*\*Emphasize climate change as a present, local, and personal risk\*\***

<!-- end list -->

1.  Mounting evidence from across the behavioral sciences has found that most **people regard climate change as a nonurgent and psychologically distant risk**—spatially, temporally, and socially—which has led to deferred public decision making about mitigation and adaptation responses.
2.  **Peoples’ sense of personal efficacy** (i.e., the belief that individual actions can make a difference) **is often very low** (Kerr & Kaufman-Gilliland, 1997). Instead, it is often more effective to appeal to and leverage the social context in which people make decisions, particularly to help promote collective efficacy (i.e., the belief that group actions can make a difference; Roser-Renouf, Maibach, Leiserowitz, & Zhao, 2014).
3.  In fact, the discounting of future risk events is a pervasive feature of the way in which human psychology evolved; **immediate day-to-day concerns take precedence over planning for the future** (van Vugt, Griskevicius, & Schultz, 2014). **As temporal distance increases, mental representations become less concrete and increasingly abstract.** Accordingly, research has found that many people view climate change as a psychologically distant, future threat (Leiserowitz, 2005; Spence, Poortinga, & Pidgeon, 2012).
4.  Research across 18 nations has found that many **people systematically judge the risks of climate change to be much more likely and more serious for other people and places than for themselves** (Gifford et al., 2009; Leiserowitz, 2005; van der Linden, 2014b).

**2. Leverage relevant social group norms**

1.  Highlighting descriptive norms such as the high degree of scientific agreement (97%) on human-caused climate change can lead to greater science acceptance and support for public action (Lewandowsky, Gignac, & Vaughan, 2013; van der Linden, Leiserowitz, Feinberg, & Maibach, 2015). 
2.  Similarly, field experiments have demonstrated that when people are informed about the average energy consumption of their neighbors, they tend to adjust their own energy use to conform to the group norm (Nolan, Schultz, Cialdini, Goldstein, & Griskevicius, 2008; Schultz, Nolan, Cialdini, Goldstein, & Griskevicius, 2007).
3.  Humans evolved living in social groups, and it is through social comparison with referent others that people validate the correctness of their opinions and decisions (Festinger, 1954). In fact, imitating the behavior of the majority (i.e., following the norm) is a common heuristic in group-living species because it reduces the cost of individual learning. **When activated and aligned, social norms can serve as powerful sources of influence**.  For example, the more people hear social referents (e.g., family and friends) **talk about the risk of climate change, and the more climate change is viewed within one’s social network as a risk that requires action, the more it amplifies an individual’s own risk perception and intention to a**ct (Renn, 2010; van der Linden, 2014b).

**3. Facilitate more effective and experiential engagement.**

1.  Statistical descriptions of the risk of climate change often fail to elicit action because statistical information, by itself, means very little to (most) people. **Experience, on the other hand, can be a powerful teacher.**

**4. Frame policy solutions in terms of what can be gained from immediate action.**

1.  **Policy frames focusing on the regionally relevant impacts of climate chang**e (and highlight local opportunities for reducing emissions) are often more effective than those that use distant global frames (e.g., Scannell & Gifford, 2013).
2.  **People are more reluctant to take action when losses are paired with uncertainty** (Tversky & Shafir, 1992)… shifting the policy conversation from the potentially negative future consequences of not acting (losses) on climate change to the positive benefits (gains) of immediate action is likely to increase public support.

**5. Appeal to intrinsically valued long-term environmental goals and outcomes.**

a) Recent experiments have shown that appealing to people’s intrinsic motivational needs can be a more effective and long-lasting driver of pro-environmental behavior (Bolderdijk, Steg, Geller, Lehman, & Postmes, 2013; van der Linden, 2015).

  

### [New Methods for New Dangers: On the Radical Practice of Listening](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1i74Ek4Mu3-NM_vWVPAeHl0UcWVT-D1l2J-ZweTxfExU/edit) *(misc. - 2019)*

  

*Article published in Climate Psychology. Studies in the Psychosocial. Palgrave Macmillan*

  

Overview: 

  - The article argues for the **need to take a hard look at our current methodologies**, and what it would look like to adopt **more innovative approaches to understanding the psycho-social dimensions of climate, energy, and environmental threats.** 
  - What assumptions are they based on, when it comes to the interplay of subjective and social influences? Are they up to the task? What might we be overlooking? 
  - Drawing on a project interviewing conservative Republicans in the United States about climate, this chapter argues that **paying attention to the “Three A’s”—Anxiety, Ambivalence, and Aspiration—can amplify our investigations, and ideally supplant a reductive tendency to focus on values alone as a key driver of behavior change.**
  - The Three A’s can be considered as a simple framework to distill the psycho-social thinking that could be used by academic and non-academic practitioners alike, particularly those crafting communications and engagement strategies. 
  - The A’s represent coexisting affective and experiential dimensions when it comes to climate change and ecological threats. The A’s often relate to tensions found in competing attachments, affiliations, identities and desires (i.e. “I’m not an environmentalist, but I am deeply concerned about the declining fish populations in our local lake and want something to be done about it”). 
  - The author has found **dialing into these Three A’s can help us in dropping the preoccupations with opinion and surface-level cognitive processes** (what we think/believe), **and focusing on what’s less conscious, yet exerting tremendous influence—what we may be feeling or sensing on cognitive, affective and somatic levels in our confrontation with our ecological crisis.** 
  - This approach is keenly interested in the places of contradiction, conflict, dilemmas, and tensions that can be conveyed through narratives. Rather than seeking continuity of values, we listen instead for the ruptures and repairs that signal areas of friction and irreconcilable tension. This has many variations and expressions, but the basic gist is the experience of “damned if you do, damned if you don’t” or being “between a rock and a hard place.” This shows up commonly in interviews and focuses group discussions as the ability to both acknowledge the issues, even if indirectly, while stating the impossibility of any meaningful form of response. 
  - The Republican Climate Project interviews were no exception. Listening to the interviews through the filter of anxiety, ambivalence and aspiration helped us uncover key themes appearing across many of them.

### [Bioethics and the Framing of Climate Change’s Health Risks](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1SqlCrM31R5cKaeIxeeqmsdLWe7omO6sO/view?usp=sharing) *(academic paper - 2015)*

*Valles, Sean A. , Bioethics 29, no. 5: 334–41.*

  - Recent empirical evidence from framing experiments indicates that **the public reacts especially positively to climate change messages framed in public health terms**.
  - Across audiences, **climate change messaging that took on a public health focus was the most likely to elicit emotional reactions consistent with support for climate change mitigation and adaptation**—more so than emphasizing risks to environment or national security
  - Recent survey indicated that **American survey respondents do not view climate change as an immediate threat to them personally**
  - The dominant mental frame used by most members of the public to organize their conceptions about climate change is that of an environmental problem, not of climate change as the enormous health problem that evidence now suggests it is
  - Switching to a health-centered frame (i.e. visual strategies and messaging) would be more pragmatically effective than a focus on imperatives to “be green”
  - Opportunity:
      
      - Giving climate change a **public health focus suggests that there is a need to both mitigate** (i.e. reduce greenhouse gas emissions) **and adapt to the problem** (i.e. protect communities and people from current and future health related impacts).
      - The **frame also presents the opportunity to involve additional trusted communication partners on the issue, notably public health experts and local community leaders, to help override public skepticism** (—example offered of bioethicists in the case of antibiotic resistance)
          
          - In the case of antimicrobial resistance, **the combination of scientific consensus and serious public health risks, communicated as a public health problem, has bypassed a network of (evolution) denialists** far older and more experienced than the climate change denialist network.

### [The Three As: Ambivalence](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bv9z6zymjH8&list=PL5CMCz5bcujvYSSLesfOusA8KhP5LG6Os&index=11) *(misc. - 2020)*

*Project InsideOut advisor Steven Malcolm Berg-Smith explains ambivalence and why it's perhaps the most important feature of how we humans relate with change. Part of the* PIO Summit: Psychological Tools for Planetary Action

  

  - Motivational Puzzle: why don’t people change, if they’re experiencing negative consequences for a specific action they are engaging in? → Ambivalence
  - Ambivalence is normal and a defining state of human experience—living in a state of extremely conflicting feelings : “We hate change and love it at the same time, what we really want is for things to remain the same and get better”
  - And yet, **ambivalence is a normal step on the road to change — ambivalence usually precedes change; it’s a gateway, an opportunity for change**
  - So, how do we engage with people who are ambivalent in a way that is helpful in supporting change? How do we help someone resolve their ambivalence in a direction that is supportive of it?
  - What’s NOT helpful:
      
      - Confronting, persuading, coaxing, pushing, convincing, telling, selling, saying: you must/should/have to/need to
      - When pressured in this way, this evokes resistance, eliciting the arguments from the other person for the case for no change
      - Which then supports that case, because people tend to become more committed to that which they give voice to (i.e. become more committed to what they hear themselves saying) → paradoxical effect
  - What IS helpful:
      
      - Suppressing the “righting reflex” — i.e., **we must learn to suppress, manage, tame our reflex that wants to make change happen, wants to fix things, advocate, persuade, convince, advocate, push**
          
          - Requires practice, and requires transforming how we think about people and connections
      - Requires being **calm, curious**
      - Deep, Empathic listening — **people are more likely to make change when people feel accurately understood**
      - Operating from a place that is accepting and **non-judgmental**
      - Recognizing, supporting, and **honoring the other person’s autonomy** and self-determination/freedom to make their own decisions — people are more likely to adopt change if they feel like they’ve authored the decision themselves
      - **Detaching ourselves from the outcome** — doesn’t mean we don’t care or don’t try our hardest, but means that at the end of an interaction, we can refrain from being emotionally attached from this person doing one thing or another, and being personally invested — if we can’t do this, we run the risk of manipulation, and suppressing the righting reflex is extremely hard
      - **Supporting people in exploring both sides of their ambivalence** — exploring ambivalence can stimulate and activate an increased motivation for change, the act frees up energy and helps unscramble doubt, awaken action
      - Focusing on and drawing out the good reasons for change — **motivation is increased when the conversation is primarily focused on/guided in the directions of the other person’s** ***own*** **reasons and arguments for change**. Requires understanding what they hear, what they value, why they might want to do something, etc.—drawing out their aspirations, wisdom, hopes and dreams.
          
          - Shifting our perspective in this way tends to help support the suppression of our righting reflex

  

### [OK Boomer: A decade of generational differences in feelings about climate change](https://drive.google.com/file/d/14_TyOmvOv6Hx65tivKZyFx9ylJl6ib2M/view) *(academic paper - 2022)*

*Study by researchers at the Pennsylvania State University, published in* Global Environmental Change

  - **Researchers analyzed survey data** of a representative sample of United States residents (*n* = 22,468 over a ten-year period (2010 to 2019) **to evaluate generational differences in emotions about climate change** and their impact on motivating people to discuss climate change with others.
  - **Younger generations’ worry about climate change increased significantly from 2010 to 2019**, as did their anger and guilt, albeit to a lesser extent. In contrast, **older generations had smaller increases in worry and no temporal changes in guilt and anger.**
  - **\*\*By 2019, average worry was more substantial than average guilt and anger.\*\* The latter of two are considered moral emotions, implying that \*\*a moral framing might not be as salient to the public as other frames.\*\***
  - **\*\*Younger generations reported less hope than older generations.\*\***
  - Interest increased over time, but did not differ by generation.
  - Differences in emotions were relatively small across categories, suggesting that **popular claims of unique emotional effects on younger generations may be overstated.**
  - **\*\*There was a strong disconnect between emotions about climate change and the frequency with which climate change was reportedly discussed.\*\***  
      - **\*\*All generations infrequently discussed climate and increases over time were small,\*\* albeit strongest for the youngest generations. Moreover, in the last year of the survey, 2019, \*\*the youngest generations were less likely to discuss climate change than Boomers and as likely to discuss climate change as the remaining generations.\*\***
      - There are at least two possible explanations for this phenomenon, which may overlap:

<!-- end list -->

1.  It has been proposed that extrinsic values and individualism have risen more among younger generations. This proposal suggests a “Me-Generation” orientation among younger generations, as reflected by increased self-focus and less civic engagement, among other trends. **Greater self-focus could account for stronger emotions about the effects of climate change, which will impact younger generations more than older generations, while simultaneously accounting for less talking with others about climate change.**
2.  Younger generations use social media more, and have had fewer in-person interactions over time. Therefore, **it is possible that social interactions about climate change are increasingly occurring on social media, rather than in-person.** These interactions may not have been fully captured in the study.

<!-- end list -->

  - Earlier findings about increasing worry moreover suggest that **many of the younger generations’ conversations about climate change may have been motivated by stress reduction, rather than by a desire to take action.**

  - **\*\*Consumers who believe that red meat is a necessary and healthy part of a diet have been found to avoid or reject information that conflicts with their beliefs.\*\***

### [(Not) Eating for the Environment: The Impact of Restaurant Menu Design on Vegetarian Food Choice](http://eprints.lse.ac.uk/87322/1/Krpan_Not%20eating%20for%20environment_2018.pdf) *(academic paper - 2018)*

  

*Research article published in* Appetite

  
  

  - *Goal:* Behavioral scientists have demonstrated that changing the context in which people act (e.g. by manipulating restaurant menu designs) shapes food choices. This study sought to explore whether and to what extent the effectiveness of these behavioral interventions is moderated by factors beyond the immediate context in which the choice is made—namely, by past eating behavior.
  - *Objective:* The study **examined whether the effectiveness of different restaurant menus in nudging pro-environmental food choice depends on the frequency at which people ate vegetarian dishes in the past** (—specifically measured by the number of days on which people reported eating only vegetarian food in the previous week, and focusing on people who are neither vegan nor vegetarian)
  - *Methodology*: In an online scenario, participants were randomly assigned to four different restaurant menu conditions—control (all dishes presented in the same manner), recommendation (vegetarian dish presented as chef’s recommendation), descriptive (more appealing description of vegetarian dish), and vegetarian (vegetarian dishes placed in a separate section)—and ordered a dish for dinner
  - *Results*:
      
      - **\*\*The results showed that the recommendation and descriptive menus increased the likelihood of vegetarian dish choices for infrequent eaters of vegetarian foods, but reduced it for those who ate vegetarian meals more often.\*\***
      - **\*\*The vegetarian menu had no impact on the infrequent vegetarian eaters’ choice, but it had a negative impact on frequent vegetarian eaters and made them less likely to order a vegetarian dish.\*\***
      - (All the results remained highly robust after testing for potential confounding influences of gender, age, BMI, and hunger.)
      - Findings indicated that people’s **past behavior is an important determinant of the impact of nudging on food choices, and that achieving sustainable eating may require more personalized interventions**.
      - Policy makers who intend to use contextual interventions to produce desirable effects on people’s food consumption or choices need to carefully consider whether these interventions can have negative consequences for certain individuals.
  - *\*Possible explanation(s):\**  
      - Moral licensing—Seeing as vegetarian foods are usually perceived as morally superior or healthier (which was shown to be the case in this experiment), the **menu interventions may have made the concept of vegetarian eating more salient, thus signaling to frequent vegetarian eaters that they have already engaged in the morally superior food choice** on numerous occasions and prompting them to select meat or fish instead

### [Communicating the benefits of agrobiodiversity enhancing products- insights from a discrete choice experiment](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1SzFne2NL62ZY0bo-w3P1uR_rrunjuj5-/view) *(academic paper - 2020)*

  

*Research article published In Gewisola*

  

  - *\*Overview:\* Agrobiodiversity is declining at a threatening rate. On-farm conservation is one prominent strategy to safeguard heirloom varieties as a crucial component of agrobiodiversity. However, cultivating those varieties is currently not attractive for farmers. Hence, a value added strategy has to be established. \*\*In this paper, we examine how the added value of heirloom varieties can be communicated to consumers by testing different communication approaches in a discrete choice experiment\*\*.* 
  - *\*Results:\* Data suggests that customers are more interested in different aspects of diversity than whether a variety is ‘old’ or not. Hence, \*\*in communicating the benefits of heirloom varieties the fact that they strengthen diversity should be a key element.\*\**
  - *\*Methodology:\**  
      - We conducted an online survey with 708 participants in Germany in 2019. The questionnaire consisted of five parts, one of which was a discrete choice experiment.
      - A discrete choice experiment is a method to analyze consumer preferences towards a certain product based on their preference towards specific attributes of that product (Hensher et al. 2015). It is based on Lancester’s “A New Approach To Consumer Theory” stating that the utility of a product is derived from the sum of the utilities of the product attributes (Lancaster, 1966) and Mc Fadden’s Random Utility Theory stating that consumers seek to maximize their utility when buying a certain product (McFadden 1974). In our discrete choice experiment, we looked at different product attributes of carrots. We chose the following attributes and attribute levels:
          
          - Price per kilogram (0.69 €, 1.29 €, 1.89 €, 2.59 €) based on market prices in different food outlets in 2019 (discounter, supermarkets, organic supermarkets and market stalls) and was set to increase by 60 ct. for each attribute level;
          - Packaging (plastic packaging, paper packaging, no packaging) based on current packaging in different food outlets;
          - Label representing the different communication approaches outlined in the introduction including a “no label” as status quo option.
      - We used a pivot design created with Ngene with 12 choice situations with three different choice cards and an additional “no choice” option. The design showed some restrictions: we used the lowest price of 0,69 € and “no label” exclusively in the status quo option which was included in every choice situation. The different labels and all packaging options were tested with the higher prices starting from 1,29 € to 2,59 €, varying in each choice situation.
      - The analysis of the choice experiment was conducted with STATA 16.
      - *Recommendations:* Results show that the label “promoter of diversity” yields the highest utility for consumers and derives the highest WTP among the labeled options. Therefore, **when communicating the benefits of heirloom varieties to consumers, the aspect of promoting diversity should be in focus rather than the age of the variety or its endangerment status**. The data suggests that **agrobiodiversity enhancing products can generate premium prices at the point of sale when the communication approach focuses on the diversity aspect**. By this generated added value, cultivating these varieties can be more attractive for farmers.

  

### [Impact of a Scalable, Multi-Campus ‘Foodprint’ Seminar on College Students’ Dietary Intake and Dietary Carbon Footprint.](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1PnzJHrzz1JjDbHvjyN-5SiSSu9d4BnQb/view?usp=sharing) *(academic paper - 2019)*

*Research published in Nutrients*

*Overview:* Prior research found a ten-unit course on food systems, and environmental sustainability shifted dietary intake and reduced dietary carbon footprint among college students.

*Results:* 

  - **Students who took the Foodprint seminar significantly improved their reported vegetable intake by 4.7 weekly servings relative to the comparison group. They also reported significantly decreasing the intake of ruminant meat and sugar-sweetened beverages.** As a result of dietary shifts, Foodprint seminar students were estimated to significantly decrease their dietary carbon footprint by 14%.
  - **The results of this pilot study suggest that a briefer, more scalable course implemented at multiple universities can yield impacts** similar to those observed in Jay et al. (2019) and Hekler et al. (2010).

*Methods:* 

  - As part of the Menus of Change University Research Collaborative, research was conducted at three university campuses in California over four academic terms. All campuses used the same curriculum, which incorporates academic readings, group discussions, and skills-based exercises to evaluate the environmental footprint of different foods. In addition to promoting healthy, sustainable food in dining operations, the group studies various campus-based interventions.
  - The comparison group comprised students taking unrelated one-unit courses at the same universities. There was no random assignment, and students voluntarily enrolled in courses and participated in the study. A questionnaire was administered at the beginning and end of each term.
  -  Dietary intake was measured using a 39-item food frequency questionnaire (FFQ). The instrument was adapted from a validated FFQ designed to measure usual food group intake among university students (unpublished, see Supplementary Material S1).
  - We assessed multiple psychosocial outcomes conceptualized as motivators for dietary behavior change, we assessed (1) climate change, (2) environmental sustainability, (3) eating a healthful diet, (4) animal rights, and (5) social justice. Items were adapted from Hekler et al. (2010) and measured using a 6-point Likert importance scale, ranging from 0 = “Not at all important” to 5 = “The very most important.” 
  - Climate change self-efficacy is intended to capture an individual’s confidence in their ability to impact climate change through their own actions and asked students to rate their level of agreement with each statement using a 5-point Likert scale, ranging from 1 = “Strongly disagree” to 5 = “Strongly agree” \[29\]. Statements included (1) “I believe my actions have an influence on climate change”, (2) “My actions to reduce the effects of climate change in my community will encourage others to reduce the effects of climate change through their own actions”, and (3) “Human beings are responsible for climate change”. 
  - For the green eating intentions the following phrasing was used: “In the next 6 months, please indicate your intention to \[behavior\].” Behaviors included (1) “Choose local/seasonal foods”, (2) “Limit processed/fast foods”, (3) “Eat meatless meals at least once/week”, (4) “Choose organic foods when possible”, (5) “Take only what you plan on eating”. Responses were measured using a 5-point Likert scale, ranging from 1 = “Definitely not” to 5 = “Definitely yes”.
  - In open-ended questions, students were asked to report the most impactful thing they learned and what (if anything) they intend to do as a result of the course.

*Other Notes:*

### [‘Don’t Tell Me What to Do’: Resistance to Climate Change Messages Suggesting 2 Behavior Changes](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1q5hAo8HNejR-skbFN3UwuBGB_78xgLMc/view?usp=sharing) *(academic paper - 2020)*

*Article published in* Weather Climate and Society

  

This study evaluates the impact of exposure to messages that emphasize the need for changes in individual behavior or in public policy to address climate change attributed to a “climate scientist” or to an unnamed source. 

  

*Method:* 

They implemented a large survey-experiment (N=1,915) online through Amazon’s Mechanical Turk (MTurk) platform that manipulated the presence of recommendations for voluntary behavioral changes or the adoption of new laws to mitigate climate change. 

  

*Results:* 

  - Regardless of the source of the information, **recommendations for behavioral changes decreased individuals’ willingness to take personal actions to reduce greenhouse gases, decreased willingness to support pro-climate candidates, reduced belief in the accelerated speed of climate change, and decreased trust in climate scientists.**
  - When messages advocate “solutions” to combat climate change, the general response was less willingness to support mitigation candidates, a reduced belief in human-induced climate change, and in the case of this message delivered by “no source”, less willingness to take personal actions to reduce emissions. 
  - In addition, **messages recommending individual behavior changes as a way to address climate change,** with or without the subtle source attribution linking the recommendation to a climate scientist, **reduced trust in climate scientists to provide accurate and impartial information.** 
  - **Messages that imply the need for individual sacrifices in living style that will be required to reduce emissions are thus translated into a negative response to the entire message, including an increased skepticism about climate science and trust in climate scientists.** Response to the messages was strongly influenced by the political identification of the respondents. 
  - This finding links back to the increasingly large set of findings that have demonstrated conservative skepticism about a variety of scientific messages, but the fact that the Independents reacted so negatively to these messages in our study warrants further study.

  

### [Two Birds, One Stone: The Effectiveness of Health and Environmental Messages to Reduce Meat Consumption and Encourage Pro-environmental Behavioral Spillover](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1jDzKUZybguzI6uZeqVB1B8h74VhjNMLA/view?usp=sharing) *(academic paper - 2020)*

  

*Article published in* Frontiers for Psychology 

  

  - This study tested the effectiveness of a randomized two-week messaging intervention on reducing red and processed meat consumption and encouraging pro-environmental behavioral spillover.
  - *\*Impetus:\* clear need to communicate the negative impacts of meat (health + climate) to raise awareness and motivate individuals to reduce their consumption. Desires to:*  
      - *1\\) Test and compare effectiveness of health versus/with environmental messaging.*
      - *2\\) Observe whether increased untargeted pro-environmental behaviors will lead to an increase in other pro-environmental behaviors.*
      - *3\\) Explore relationship between pro-environmental behavior + identity*
  - *Methodology*: undergraduate students in the UK (320) randomly allocated to four conditions in which they received information about the 1) health, 2) environmental, or 3) combined (health and environmental) impacts of meat consumption, and a 4) no-message control
  - *\*Results:\* \*\*receiving info on health and/or environmental impacts of meat was effective in reducing consumption\*\*, as compared to the control group (further \*\*supporting existing evidence of the effectiveness of informational strategies), but little evidence of behavioral spillover/effect on pro-environmental identity\*\**  
      - What *was* observed, however, was that providing information on the environmental and the combined environmental and health impacts of meat was particularly effective in encouraging further dietary change, compared to providing information only on the health impacts of meat.
      - And the intervention did not have any significant effects on pro-environmental identity (—a positive finding, in that the intervention did not result in any inadvertent increase in negative environmental impacts) and that pro-environmental identity did not have any significant effect on participants’ willingness to engage in different pro- environmental behaviors.

### [Perceptions of behaviors that cause and mitigate global warming and intentions to perform these behaviors](https://drive.google.com/drive/u/2/folders/12Z9hOMZ_k1MkSqiL0Fvym9dxkvD65jTa) *(academic paper - 2012)*

  

  - This paper investigates people’s knowledge of household and travel behaviors and perceptions of these behaviors’ impact in causing and mitigating climate change.

  

  - *Method:* In the present study, a sample of college students (N = 112) completed several surveys on the computer individually on the internet from their residences. It was asked to list the behaviors they perform that cause global warming (GW) and the behaviors they could perform to mitigate GW, to rate the impact of the behaviors in terms of their effect on causing or mitigating GW, and to rate their intention to perform each of the behaviors. 

  

  - *Results:* This study is the first we know of to investigate the influences of effectiveness knowledge and effectiveness beliefs on intention to perform behaviors that mitigate climate change. **Effective knowledge was not consistently associated with intentions to perform behaviors that mitigate climate change.** We found that effectiveness knowledge only significantly correlated with intention to purchase a more fuel-efficient car.

  

  - **On the other hand, the perceived effectiveness of a particular behavior had a major influence on intention to perform that behavior for all behaviors under investigation** (whether actual mitigators or not). As would be expected from the Theory of Planned Behavior (Ajzen, 1991; Ajzen & Fishbein, 2005), **stronger belief that a behavior effectively mitigated GW led to stronger intentions to adopt that behavior in the future.** 

  

  - Effectiveness beliefs, as conceptualized in the current study, are considered as background variables in the Theory of Planned Behavior, influencing intention only indirectly through attitude. But, effectiveness beliefs are also closely related to personal response efficacy beliefs, or outcome expectancy beliefs, as identified by Bandura (1977).

### [Targeting interventions to distinct meat-eating groups reduces meat consumption](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1AHitayZXpYhmv2YhFD3I5o1l01VnPlsh/view) *(academic paper - 2020)*

*By researchers at the University of Victoria, published in* Food Quality and Preference

  - Researchers sorted study participants into three groups, based on dietary behavior:

<!-- end list -->

1.  *Strong-hindrance meat eaters* (highest baseline meat consumption)
2.  *Moderate-hindrance meat eaters* (lower baseline meat consumption)
3.  *Meat-reducers* (lowest baseline meat consumption)

<!-- end list -->

  - They then designed three separate meat reduction intervention conditions, each intended to address one specific group’s meat consumption inhibitors:

<!-- end list -->

1.  *Information-and-substitution condition*
      
    1.  Designed for strong-hindrance meat eaters
    2.  Included news article introducing the New Canada Food Guide, social norm, and suggested red meat substitution
2.  *Information-and-healthy-recipe condition*
      
    1.  Designed for moderate-hindrance meat eaters
    2.  Included news article introducing the New Canada Food Guide, social norm, and suggested healthy recipes
3.  *Implementation-intention condition*
      
    1.  Designed for meat-reducers
    2.  Included implementation intention exercise around reducing meat consumption

<!-- end list -->

  - Participants in the treatment group were randomly assigned to one of these three conditions, meaning that several participants received conditions that were mismatched (i.e., not specifically designed for their group)
  - Compared to control, participants in the overall treatment group reduced their GHG-weighted animal product consumption by 20 g of CO2e per day on average, equivalent to about replacing one portion of pork with chicken once per week

  - This study **illustrates the importance of designing targeted meat reduction interventions that match their intended audience**
  - **\*\*For meat-eaters who are not actively working to reduce meat consumption, interventions should focus on increasing their perception of the benefits of reducing meat consumption and on increasing their behavioral interventions\*\***
  - **\*\*For those already working to reduce meat consumption, targeted interventions should focus on supporting existing reduction efforts\*\***

  

### [Accelerating Consumer Adoption of Plant-Based Meat: An Evidence-Based Guide for Effective Practice](https://gfi.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/01/NO-HYPERLINKED-REFERENCES-FINAL-COMBINED-accelerating-consumer-adoption-of-plant-based-meat.pdf) *(report - 2020)*

*Produced by researchers from The Good Food Institute and Yale University*

  - This 111-page publication was primarily intended to serve as **a practical resource to inform product development and marketing strategies for those working in the plant-based meat sector**, as well as to provide a “launching point” for actionable research to identify further strategies to promote consumer adoption
  - Researchers conducted a **comprehensive literature review to determine inductively the most effective strategies for accelerating consumer adoption of plant-based meat**
  - They divided this topic into five “chapters”: (1) food-choice; (2) consumer segmentation; (3) product attributes and product development; (4) choice architecture; and (5) messaging

<!-- end list -->

1.  Food-Choice Motivations
      
    1.  The **three foundational motivations for food choice are taste, cost, and convenience**
    2.  **If these three core drivers are met, consumers then have the opportunity to incorporate their higher values into their food choices** (including health, sustainability, and animal welfare)
    3.  For traditional meat consumers, health, weight loss, and cost serve as motivations to reduce meat consumption
    4.  For meat reducers (“flexitarians”), health is the primary driver, with environmental impact and animal welfare as secondary drivers
    5.  For vegetarians/vegans, health, environmental impact, and animal welfare all serve as motivations
    6.  These findings suggest that **developing plant-based meat products that are delicious, easy to purchase and prepare, familiar, and less expensive and healthier than conventional meat** (with comparable protein content) **will be an effective avenue to increasing plant-based meat consumption** in the majority of the population
    7.  The above benefits should be promoted through targeted marketing
    8.  Appeals to sustainability and animal welfare alone will be effective only for a small portion of the general population
2.  Consumer Segmentation
      
    1.  The authors **recommend segmenting consumers by the adopter categories of Roger’s Diffusion of Innovations Theory** (innovators, early adopters, early majority, late majority, and laggards)
    2.  It is **most practical to separate a population by its current rate of meat consumption in order to most effectively target for plant-based meat adoption** (i.e., vegetarians/vegans, meat reducers, and traditional meat consumers)
    3.  **Targeting the meat reducer (“flexitarian”) segment will be the most effective use of resources because this group is already open to changing its behavior**
    4.  Marketers should be sure that messages targeting the above group do not create reactance among the larger traditional meat consumer segment
    5.  **Flexitarians’ adoption of plant-based meat would lead the way for wider societal adoption** 
3.  Product Attributes and Product Development

<!-- end list -->

1.  The **top motivations for food choice** that should be considered in product development **include taste and other sensory characteristics, price, convenience, familiarity or novelty, and health or nutritional profile**
2.  The **perceived strengths of plant-based meat** that product developers and marketers should leverage **include health benefits, appropriateness within meal contexts, status as “new” and “exciting,” and, to a lesser extent, low environmental impact and high animal welfare impact**
3.  **Current reported consumer barriers to consumption of plant-based meat** that product developers and marketers need to overcome **include negative health beliefs, lack of familiarity with the product, perceived high cost, low sensory appeal, and inconvenience**
4.  **Plant-based meat products should be developed to provide personal benefits to the flexitarian consumer, such as improved taste and other sensory aspects, lower product cost, increased product convenience, and improved healthiness of the product. The product should be exciting yet provide a strong sense of familiarity**
5.  Improved sensory experience is likely to be achieved by developing products that are closer to conventional meat in texture, juiciness, and appearance
6.  Regarding health beliefs, consumers perceive plant-based meat as healthy in terms of facilitating weight loss and being low in saturated fat but also express uncertainty in terms of sufficient protein or nutrient content and digestibility, especially in comparison with conventional meat
7.  Regarding the “newness” of plant-based meat, a portion of the population dislikes trying new foods, and thus, to access these individuals, marketers should frame plant-based meat as familiar
8.  Another portion of the population perceives new foods as an enjoyable adventure, and thus, to access these individuals, marketers should highlight the products’ status as new and exciting when framing them

  

1.  Choice Architecture
      
    1.  **Nudge strategies to motivate food behavior include product placement at a grocery store, labels on products, listing a food item first or last on a menu, using a “default” ingredient on a menu, providing menu item descriptions, or a combination of these strategies**
    2.  For product placement, **plant-based meat can be strategically placed where it will be more convenient for consumers to purchase**, such as adjacent to the conventional meat section
    3.  For labeling, **health and environmental labels on product packages and in menus** (e.g., red-green-yellow traffic light labeling for calorie count) **can be useful nudges for those who currently limit meat consumption**
    4.  Furthermore, **describing a product as “veggie \_\_\_\_\_” or “\[type of meat\]-less” does not appeal to most consumers. Terms like “plant-based” or “plant protein” are more effective, as are labels that highlight protein and fiber content or familiarity, such as “all-American”**
    5.  **Menu item descriptions that are more appealing and detailed** (e.g., highlighting a product’s taste or its ingredients’ geographical origin) **increase sales of vegetarian menu items in a restaurant setting**
    6.  **Menu-design structure can increase selection of plant-based meat through the availability of more plant-based options, default choices, a chef’s recommendation box, an integrated menu, or placement of plant-based meat dishes first or last on a menu**

  

1.  Messaging
      
    1.  **\*\*When preparing a marketing strategy, consider not only the content of the message but the message source, channel, target audience, and framing\*\***  
        1.  *Message source*: The message source plays an important role in influencing consumer attitudes and openness to a message
        2.  *Communication channel*: To reach a specific audience, message designers must find out to which communication media the target audience is most exposed
        3.  *Targeted messages*: A market strategy’s effectiveness in influencing consumers strongly depends on the preferences, habits, and behaviors of the target audience
        4.  *Framing*: Message designers should choose a benefit frame that will most widely appeal to their target audience’s needs or wants
    2.  **\*\*Applying tested behavioral and social influence theories to message design and dissemination increases the likelihood of achieving desired behavioral outcomes\*\***  
        1.  *Integrative Model:* An effective influence strategy utilizes (1) messages that appeal to the target consumers’ attitudes toward eating plant-based meat, (2) messages that demonstrate to target consumers that most people similar to them eat plant-based meat, or (3) encouragement and instructions regarding preparation of plant-based meat.
        2.  *Self-efficacy:* People’s beliefs about their capability determine how they feel, think, motivate themselves, and behave. Messaging focused on providing easy-preparation instructions, including noted similarities to conventional meat preparation when applicable, may address this barrier
        3.  *Transtheoretical Model:* An effective way to develop targeted messages is to base them on consumers’ stages of change
        4.  *Theory of Planned Behavior:* An effective strategy for influencing behavior is to target three key variables: perceived social pressure, belief that the behavior is within one’s control, and (especially) attitudes toward the behavior
        5.  *Social influence:* Social norms messaging is an especially promising area of influence and should be tested in the specific context of plant-based meat promotion and adoption.
        6.  *Types of social norms:* In the context of plant-based meat, descriptive norms are likely to be more effective than injunctive norms 
        7.  *Dynamic descriptive social norms:* Framing descriptive norms as dynamic (popularity has increased over time) or as dynamic with future growth (popularity has increased over time and is expected to increase even more) is an especially promising message content application to plant-based meat.
    3.  **\*\*When designing messages to increase consumer adoption of plant-based meat, choose the message content most likely to drive purchasing\*\***  
        1.  *Taste and sensory appeal:* Message content related to taste will most strongly appeal to consumers
        2.  *Familiarity:* Traditional meat consumers and meat reducers tend to be more interested in foods that they find traditional, familiar, or comforting
        3.  *Convenience:* Messaging that describes plant-based meat as convenient and easy to prepare, suited to the broader meal context, and similar to conventional meat (where applicable) is likely to appeal to the widest audience
        4.  *Health benefits:* Messages about plant-based meat’s health benefits should typically frame these benefits as a positive gain, not an absence of a negative. High protein content should be the central point highlighted in health-focused marketing messages
        5.  *Altruistic benefits:* Altruistic benefits, such as environmental friendliness and animal welfare, are unlikely to significantly drive purchasing among traditional meat consumers. They are somewhat more effective for active meat reducers but still fall well below the other attributes
        6.  *Social norms:* The most compelling social norms are dynamic descriptive norms and future-growth dynamic norms

  

### [Interindividual differences in environmentally relevant positive trait affect impacts sustainable behavior in everyday life](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1D1rndvpkZVOSrZ2tN4O6ryB7LLASWE9m/view) *(academic paper - 2021)*

*By researchers at the University of Geneva, published in* Nature Portfolio

  - In two experiments, researchers explored the relationship between individual predispositions to experience positive emotions (trait affect) and pro-environmental actions, as well as corresponding shifts in affective states
  - Their first experiment showed that **high levels of positive trait affect are associated with (1) a higher number of committed positive environmentally relevant behaviors (ERBs), and (2) stronger shifts in positive affective state after committing positive ERBs, as well as after being exposed to positive ERBs**
  - Additionally, **low levels of positive affect were associated with more negative affective shifts after committing positive ERBs**
  - Their second experiments showed that **participants with higher levels of trait affect experienced higher average levels of positive emotions when exposed to environmentally positive news, as well as lower levels of positive emotions when exposed to environmentally negative news**
  - Additionally, **participants with high trait affect who read a communication about positive environmental news events were more likely to report committing a positive ERB** compared to those who read negative environmental news or non-environmental news
  - Furthermore, **participants with high levels of trait affect who were exposed to positive environmental news in the morning had a higher likelihood to commit positive ERBs throughout the rest of the day.** However, **participants with low levels of trait affect who were exposed to positive environmental news in the morning had a lower likelihood to commit positive ERBs**
  - These findings can help inform the design of effective affect-based interventions aiming to promote sustainable behavior

  

### [Complex Behavioral Challenges Require Multi-Faceted Behavioral Solutions: Driving Change in Sustainable Agriculture](https://drive.google.com/file/d/12nY5VJ3DJxEoIQ3zOElHwuNT7W-JytZW/view) *(report - 2021)*

*\*\*Starts on page 122\*\* - a featured article of the 2021 Behavioral Economics Guide*

  - The authors assert that **behavioral science-driven programming should move beyond a singular focus on choice architecture through marginal nudges, and towards intensive, multi-faceted, and behaviorally-informed solutions necessary for addressing pressing, wicked, and/or complex problems** of our time.
  - Justifiable criticisms of a narrow and/or excessive focus on nudging include the following:
      
      - **\*\*Nudges tend to beget relatively small effects.\*\***
      - **\*\*Effects of nudges tend to decay significantly over time.\*\***
      - **\*\*Nudges are often deployed homogeneously in ways that are not reflective of heterogeneous populations, thus decreasing the nudges’ effectiveness.\*\***
  - One example of **a successful multi-faceted and multi-layered behavioral program is the Lands for Life (L4L) program**, designed by the environmental behavioral change non-profit Rare.
      
      - The program’s focus was getting smallholders farmers in Colombia to adopt climate-friendly practices, in spite of strong negative norms in favor of intensive production practices.
      - This group of farmers was quite diverse, such that a homogeneous nudge would likely not have adequately captured the population (though even if it did, marginal behavioral impacts from a nudge would not have been sufficiently impactful at a landscape level).
  - Rare sought to design a behaviorally-informed program that:

<!-- end list -->

1.  **\*\*Adapted to farmers’ differing needs and attitudes\*\***
2.  **\*\*Generated new, positive norms around sustainability in farming communities\*\***
3.  **\*\*Succeeded in getting a\*\* \*\*\*localized-but-ever-increasing\*\*\* \*\*number of farmers to adopt climate-friendly practices\*\***

<!-- end list -->

  - Rare’s program focused on three target behaviors.
      
    1.  Fertilizing according to individual need
    2.  Irrigating according to individual need
    3.  Enriching soil with compost
  - Rare’s program **targeted farmers with low, medium, and high levels of resistance to ambiguity**, the latter group being the most resistant to adopting new, unfamiliar practices.

<!-- end list -->

  - For those with low levels of resistance to ambiguity, simplicity and accessibility of the program were to be prioritized.
  - For those with medium levels of resistance, descriptive norms were identified as being important, with farmers being more likely to adopt new behaviors if they knew that others had.
  - For those with high levels of resistance, supplemental gains and/or losses were prioritized as important to changing behavior. These could include injunctive norms, such as the community thinking that farmers should be adopting novel practices because that would be best for the community. 

<!-- end list -->

  - Given the above theoretical framework, **a three-phased program was implemented:**

<!-- end list -->

1.  **\*\*Invest heavily in an early cohort of\*\* \*\*\*innovadores\*\*\* \*\*(farmer innovators).\*\***
2.  **\*\*Leverage the social proof they provide the community to set a change of norm in motion.\*\***
3.  **\*\*Leverage the ever-growing number of\*\* \*\*\*innovadores\*\*\* \*\*and their families to reinforce that the community now expects farmers to farm sustainably.\*\***

### [The Language of Sustainable Diets: A Field Study Exploring the Impact of Renaming Vegetarian Dishes on UK Cafe Menus](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1eVe5pwJfe6gD6w2jREpz2c3utEpF8O_9/view?usp=sharing) *(report - 2018)*
